name: Ben Gordon
milestone_by_age_26: Selected 3rd overall in the 2004 NBA Draft by the Chicago Bulls at age 21 after leading UConn to the 2004 NCAA championship; as a rookie (age 21–22) became the first player to win NBA Sixth Man of the Year as a rookie and made the All-Rookie First Team.
early_history_summary: Born in London to a Jamaican father and African-American mother; raised in Mount Vernon, New York. Starred at Mount Vernon High School (state championships), then UConn (2001–2004), earning Big East tournament MVP and helping win the 2004 national title before entering the NBA draft after his junior year.
family_context_summary: Born in London; father Jamaican, mother African-American; family moved to Mount Vernon, New York when he was an infant. Detailed family financial status not documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as basketball-domain coaching family in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: UConn basketball, NBA draft pipeline, high-school state titles, scoring talent, early pro declaration
evidence_summary: Gordon's path was classic elite American basketball: Mount Vernon high-school stardom, UConn national championship at ~21, then #3 NBA pick and historic Sixth Man of the Year as a rookie. Advantage was primarily physical talent plus institutional pipeline (UConn/Big East/NBA), not family capital or inherited networks. Later multi-team NBA career and mental-health advocacy after retirement.
starting_point: Born in London to Jamaican and African-American parents; raised from infancy in Mount Vernon, New York in a basketball-focused youth environment.
current_position: Former NBA player (2004–2015+); inducted into UConn Huskies of Honor (2025); public advocate on bipolar disorder and mental health after retirement.

trajectory.event: Helped Mount Vernon High School win New York State Public and Federation Championships as an All-State recruit.
Led UConn to the NCAA championship, won Big East tournament MVP, and was selected 3rd overall by the Chicago Bulls in the NBA Draft.
Won NBA Sixth Man of the Year as a rookie—the first player ever to do so—and made All-Rookie First Team.
Signed a multi-year free-agent deal with the Detroit Pistons after five seasons as Chicago's primary scorer.
Publicly detailed bipolar disorder and mental-health struggles in The Players' Tribune after retirement.
Inducted into the UConn Huskies of Honor.

name: Brad Cox
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Furman University B.S. (~1965, age ~21); Ph.D. University of Chicago 1973 (~age 29); Objective-C created early 1980s (~age 36–40) with Tom Love; Stepstone founded later.
early_history_summary: Grew up on a dairy farm in Lake City, South Carolina; earned organic chemistry and mathematics degrees at Furman (class of 1965), then a Ph.D. in mathematical biology at the University of Chicago (1973). Early work included neural-set simulation (1971 paper) and NIH/Woods Hole research before software language design.
family_context_summary: Born Fort Benning, Georgia; raised on a South Carolina dairy farm. Parents Nancy Hinson Cox and Dewey McBride Cox per obituary sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as computing/software domain family.
evidence_summary: Cox's defining achievement—Objective-C and Stepstone—came in his late 30s. Pre-26 record is undergraduate education; Ph.D. and research publications arrived after age 26. No independently dated material software milestone by 26 found.

name: Nikolaos Bourbakis
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Born 1950; B.Sc. mathematics University of Athens 1974 (~age 23–24); Ph.D. computer engineering University of Patras 1983 (~age 32–33). IEEE CS Technical Achievement Award 1998 (~age 48).
early_history_summary: Born in Chania, Crete; studied mathematics in Athens then electrical/computer engineering at Patras, completing a Ph.D. in 1983. Later career in image processing, assistive tech, and as Ohio Board of Regents Distinguished Professor at Wright State University.
evidence_summary: Bourbakis's documented research awards and faculty distinction occur well after age 26. Pre-26 record is standard undergraduate mathematics study; Ph.D. at ~33 is the first clear career credential and is past the cutoff.

name: Mu Li
milestone_by_age_26: No verified material milestone by age 26 with a documented birth year. Entered SJTU ACM class ~2004; Baidu researcher ~2011–2012; CMU Ph.D. 2012–2017; MXNet arXiv paper 2015 (widely cited deep-learning framework). Without confirmed birth year, cannot verify age ≤26 for MXNet or Baidu roles; conservative ineligible.
early_history_summary: Chinese deep-learning researcher; SJTU computer science (ACM class) undergraduate path from 2004, early Baidu IDL research roles, then CMU Ph.D. under Alex Smola (completed 2017) with work on scaling distributed ML. Co-authored MXNet (2015); later Amazon principal scientist and Boson AI co-founder/CTO.
evidence_summary: MXNet (2015) and CMU Ph.D. (2017) are the clearest breakout credentials and almost certainly post-26 given a typical ~1986 birth cohort from 2004 undergrad entry. No primary-source birth date found; eligibility cannot be certified under strict age rules.

name: Craig Silverstein
milestone_by_age_26: Joined Google in 1998 as its first hire (employee #1 after founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin) at about age 25–26 while a Stanford Ph.D. student, becoming a core systems/search engineer and later director of technology.
early_history_summary: Harvard undergraduate (ACM-ICPC world champion team 1993); Stanford CS Ph.D. student under Rajeev Motwani alongside Page and Brin. Helped with Google when it was still a Stanford project, then became the company's first full-time employee at incorporation (1998). Served as technology director until 2012, then joined Khan Academy.
family_context_summary: Parents Burton and Janet referenced in secondary biography sources; detailed class/financial background not richly documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented as computing-domain parental expertise.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Harvard, Stanford Motwani group, Page/Brin peers, ICPC, early web search wave
evidence_summary: Silverstein combined elite CS training (Harvard ICPC champion; Stanford Ph.D. track) with direct adjacency to Page and Brin in Motwani's group, becoming Google's first hire at ~25–26 (confirmed age ~35 in 2008 press). He contributed core search/systems work for ~14 years, then moved to Khan Academy education infrastructure and Giving Pledge philanthropy with his wife.
starting_point: Not fully documented; elite U.S. education path via Harvard then Stanford CS Ph.D. program in the 1990s.
current_position: Former Google director of technology and first employee; long-time Khan Academy infrastructure leader; Giving Pledge signer with spouse Mary Obelnicki.

trajectory.event: Won the ACM-ICPC world championship as a member of the Harvard University programming team.
Joined Google as its first employee (after Page and Brin) at company founding, working on search and systems from the Menlo Park garage era.
Serving as Google technology director on the company's 10th anniversary, still a core technical leader.
Left Google after ~14 years to join education nonprofit Khan Academy as a senior engineer/leader.
Continued education-tech and philanthropy work; listed among Giving Pledge signers with spouse.

name: Andy Hunt
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 verifiable: birth year not documented in reviewed sources. Defining works—The Pragmatic Programmer (1999) and Agile Manifesto (2001)—cannot be age-dated without birth year; Wikipedia lists year of birth missing.
early_history_summary: American programmer and author; co-wrote The Pragmatic Programmer with Dave Thomas (1999), co-founded the Pragmatic Bookshelf, and was one of 17 original Agile Manifesto authors (2001). Later books on agile practices and thinking/learning; also musician.
evidence_summary: Without a documented birth year, age-at-milestone cannot be computed for The Pragmatic Programmer or the Agile Manifesto. Strict eligibility requires a dated ≤26 milestone; marked ineligible.

name: Keith Schacht
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Lever Works in college and sold it to Leo Media in December 2001 at age 22; co-founded Inventables in 2002 at age 22–23 (materials/innovation platform featured in Forbes/Wired); named among BusinessWeek top 20 entrepreneurs under 25; TED speaker by 2005 (age 25).
early_history_summary: American entrepreneur (born 9 Dec 1979); University of Illinois Urbana–Champaign. Built and sold custom software firm Lever Works while still in college, then co-founded Inventables with Zach Kaplan, spoke at TED, founded Facebook-platform company Crafted Fun, later product-managed Facebook News Feed, and co-founded Mystery Science (YC, sold to Discovery Education for $140M in 2020).
primary_early_advantage_tags: college cofounders, UIUC, Inventables, TED, serial entrepreneurship
evidence_summary: Schacht repeatedly founded and exited companies starting in college: Lever Works sale at 22, Inventables at 22–23, TED by 25, then Facebook PM and Mystery Science ($140M acquisition). Early advantage looks like high-trust cofounder teams and execution reps rather than inherited capital; family background undocumented.
starting_point: Not documented in reviewed sources beyond U.S. origin and University of Illinois education.
current_position: Serial entrepreneur and angel investor; co-founder of Mystery Science (acquired by Discovery Education for $140M in 2020); investor in companies including Credit Karma, Canva, and others.

trajectory.event: Sold college-founded custom software firm Lever Works to Leo Media (cofounded with Brian Witlin and Zach Kaplan).
Co-founded Inventables, a materials/innovation company later featured in Forbes and Wired.
Spoke at TED on materials/toys from the future; named among BusinessWeek top young entrepreneurs.
Joined Facebook as product manager; helped launch an updated News Feed in 2011; named inventor on multiple patents.
Co-founded Mystery Science with Doug Peltz to deliver elementary science lessons.
Mystery Science acquired by Discovery Education for $140 million; Schacht majority shareholder at sale.

name: Bonnie Berger
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Machtey Award (best student paper) at FOCS 1989 at about age 24 for work on parallel algorithms with John Rompel; completed MIT Ph.D. in 1990 (age ~25) under Silvio Micali, then stayed at MIT for postdoc and joined the faculty in 1992.
early_history_summary: Raised in Miami; father encouraged early math, mother later led Jewish education organizations. BA Brandeis 1983 (switched into new CS program after Fortran class); MIT SM 1986 / PhD 1990 (Micali). Pivoted from algorithms to computational molecular biology in postdoc with Daniel Kleitman; became a founding figure in computational biology at MIT CSAIL.
family_context_summary: Miami Jewish family; paternal grandfather Russian immigrant; father businessman and classically trained pianist; mother Helene Berger later headed Jewish Education Service of North America. Father strongly encouraged early mathematics.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father provided early math encouragement; not a professional CS/comp-bio apprenticeship, but intellectual support.
primary_early_advantage_tags: MIT PhD, FOCS Machtey Award, Micali advisor, Brandeis early CS, father math encouragement
evidence_summary: Berger showed early math drive in Miami, finished Brandeis CS in 1983, then earned an MIT Ph.D. by ~25 with a FOCS Machtey Award at ~24—clear ≤26 research milestones. Mentorship (Micali, informal Peter Shor, postdoc Kleitman) and MIT pipeline steered her into founding-level computational biology. Later NAS member, ACM Fellow, and major genomics/privacy contributions.
starting_point: Born and raised in Miami in a Jewish family; father (businessman/pianist) encouraged early mathematics; mother later a national Jewish education leader.
current_position: Simons Professor of Mathematics at MIT; head of Computation and Biology group at MIT CSAIL; National Academy of Sciences member; major figure in computational biology and genomic privacy.

trajectory.event: Earned BA from Brandeis University after switching into the university's new computer science program.
Won the FOCS Machtey Award for best student paper on parallel algorithms (with John Rompel).
Completed MIT Ph.D. in computer science under Silvio Micali and began postdoctoral work pivoting toward computational biology.
Joined MIT faculty as assistant professor of applied mathematics with a joint LCS appointment.
Named to MIT Technology Review TR100 innovators list for computational biology work.
Elected ACM Fellow.
Elected to the National Academy of Sciences; delivered AWM-SIAM Sonia Kovalevsky Lecture.

name: Thibaut Lavril
milestone_by_age_26: No material dated milestone by age 26 verified. École Polytechnique engineering studies ~2010–2014; later Meta/FAIR co-author on LLaMA (2023) and related LLM work; subsequently Mistral AI. Without confirmed birth year and pre-26 breakout publication/role, marked ineligible.
early_history_summary: French AI engineer; diplôme d'ingénieur path via École Polytechnique (physics & applied mathematics, ~2010–2014) with study abroad in Brazil. Research/engineering roles leading to co-authorship on Meta's LLaMA open foundation models (2023); later AI research engineer at Mistral AI.
evidence_summary: LLaMA (2023) is the clear public breakout and almost certainly post-26 given a Polytechnique 2010–2014 cohort. No Wikipedia biography with birth date; strict age-26 eligibility not met on available evidence.

name: Charlie Cheever
milestone_by_age_26: Joined Facebook in January 2006 at age 24 as an early engineer/manager after Amazon; contributed to News Feed, Facebook Connect, Gaming, and Video, and built internal tool BunnyLol—material early-platform engineering milestone before co-founding Quora at 27.
early_history_summary: Born Pittsburgh (Aug 2, 1981); Shady Side Academy; Harvard CS BA 1999–2003 (Fly Club). Built a Harvard student dorm database in 2000 that drew Administrative Board attention and is cited as partial inspiration for Zuckerberg's early experiments. Worked at Amazon Seattle, then was recruited to early Facebook; left in 2009 to co-found Quora with Adam D'Angelo.
family_context_summary: Pittsburgh origin; attended elite private Shady Side Academy. Detailed parental occupation/wealth not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Harvard CS, early Facebook hire, D'Angelo partnership, social platform wave, Amazon experience
evidence_summary: Cheever's ≤26 milestone is early Facebook engineering leadership at 24 on products used at global scale, after Harvard CS and Amazon. Advantage stack is elite education plus peer network (Zuckerberg recruitment; later D'Angelo cofounder), not family domain apprenticeship. Quora (2009) and Expo (mid-2010s) are major post-26 founder outcomes.
starting_point: Born in Pittsburgh; attended Shady Side Academy and Harvard (CS BA 2003); early experiments building student-information tools at college.
current_position: Co-founder/president of Expo (React Native app platform); Quora co-founder and advisor; works on castle.xyz creative tools.

trajectory.event: Built a Harvard student-body dorm database that was shut down by the administration and later cited as an influence on Zuckerberg's early projects.
Graduated Harvard with a B.A. in Computer Science; joined Amazon as a programmer in Seattle.
Joined Facebook as an early engineer/manager; contributed to News Feed, Connect, Gaming, and Video.
Left Facebook to co-found Quora with Adam D'Angelo.
Stepped back from day-to-day Quora management while remaining an advisor.
Began building Expo (then Exponent), an open-source universal app platform using React Native.

name: Leah Silber
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 verifiable: birth year not found in reviewed sources. Known for Ember.js core team, Tilde Inc. co-founding, and organizing RailsConf/EmberConf/GoGaRuCo—milestones cannot be age-dated without birth year.
early_history_summary: Open-source community leader and CEO of Tilde Inc.; Ember.js core team member; organizer of EmberConf, RailsConf, GoGaRuCo; author of Event Driven (guide to tech events). Background in startup marketing and OSS community building (jQuery, Bundler, Merb).
evidence_summary: Silber is a well-known Ember/Rails community leader, but public sources lack birth year and dated pre-26 breakout events. Strict eligibility requires a dated ≤26 milestone; marked ineligible.

name: Ilkay Altintas
milestone_by_age_26: No material breakout milestone by age 26 found. BS METU 1999 (~22), MS 2001 (~24); joined SDSC as research programmer in 2001 (~24). Ph.D. University of Amsterdam 2011 (~34). Kepler scientific workflow system major paper 2006 (~29). WIFIRE and chief data science officer roles later.
early_history_summary: Born Aydın, Turkey (1977); METU computer engineering BS/MS; hired at San Diego Supercomputer Center in 2001. Co-initiated Kepler scientific workflow system; Ph.D. on collaborative provenance (Amsterdam, 2011). Founded WIFIRE wildfire cyberinfrastructure; became SDSC chief data science officer (2015).
evidence_summary: Early SDSC hire at ~24 is solid career start but not an independently notable breakout. Kepler's widely cited 2006 paper and later WIFIRE/CDSO leadership are post-26. Conservative ineligible under material-milestone rule.
